The distribution is useful for repeated mixed-flow testing. While testing one route, you may temporarily increase the probability of the relevant product type instead of waiting for it to occur randomly. Restore the intended distribution before validating the complete system.

title: Conveyor System
section: Build and configure one sorting station
text:
Build and configure one sorting station
Place an incoming Conveyor, one Pusher Conveyor, and one side Conveyor. Position the configured feeder at the beginning of the incoming Conveyor, then connect all compatible interfaces and check that the path directions are consistent. Leave enough straight path before the pusher for products to enter its detection region reliably.
Configure the physical properties that should be common to every station, such as conveyor dimensions, height, and speed. On the Pusher Conveyor, set RouteBy to RoutingRule, open the RoutingRule editor, select Product Type Rule, and set the default connection to Out. Do not assign a product type yet.
Run the simulation and confirm that products pass through the station without jumping, rotating unexpectedly, or becoming stuck at an interface. Correct the common settings before creating copies.

title: Conveyor System
section: Duplicate and connect the sorting stations
text:
Duplicate and connect the sorting stations
Select the configured Pusher Conveyor together with its side Conveyor and duplicate the pair three times. Connect the straight Out interface of each Pusher Conveyor to the input of the next one, forming a line of four sorting stations. Add an ordinary conveyor after the final Out connection for the grey cylinders.
Because the shared physical settings and the Product Type Rule were configured before duplication, only the station-specific routing now needs to be changed. Adjust spacing or conveyor lengths where needed, then run products through the complete line once with all four rules still using their default Out route.

title: Conveyor System
section: Configure run control for the ordinary conveyors
text:
Configure run control for the ordinary conveyors
Use one of the ordinary conveyors’ existing Boolean PowerOnSignal values as the shared run command:

Select an ordinary conveyor and show its component signals.
Draw signal connections from its PowerOnSignal to the PowerOnSignal of each remaining ordinary conveyor.
Use the selected conveyor’s signal as the single run command for the line.

Change the shared value manually and verify that all connected paths start and stop together. Test this again after resetting the simulation. Some component behaviors react when a signal value changes, so explicitly toggle the command once rather than assuming that its initial value has already been applied.
Do not connect this signal to the Pusher Conveyor’s One-WayPath. Its internal script temporarily stops and restarts that path while transferring a product. Connecting another signal to the same Enabled property would create two independent writers whose commands can overwrite one another.
The shared signal provides one clear line-level command for the ordinary conveyors. It can later be mapped to the PLC without mapping those conveyors separately.

title: Conveyor System
text:
Configure internal pusher routing
The standard Pusher Conveyor contains internal logic that detects, attaches, moves, and transfers a product to the selected outgoing path. Use that complete behavior at each station:

At pusher 1, assign Cylinder_blue to Pusher.
At pusher 2, assign Cylinder_red to Pusher.
At pusher 3, assign Cylinder_green to Pusher.
At pusher 4, assign Cylinder_purple to Pusher.
Keep Out as the default connection in every rule so that all other product types continue to the next station.

Do not replace this behavior by controlling only the visible pusher joint. The joint motion alone does not perform the product attachment and transfer between conveyor paths.
Run the system until every product type has passed through the sorting line. Confirm that each coloured type leaves at its assigned side conveyor and that grey cylinders pass all four pushers and continue through the final outlet.

title: Conveyor System
text:
Possible extension: PLC-controlled pushing
Full PLC control of the push cycle requires a tested interface that requests one complete transfer and receives completion feedback. Directly commanding the pusher joint is not sufficient.
Full PLC control of the push cycle is not part of the required stage. Treat it as an extension only after the required conveyor and robot-cell coordination works reliably.

title: Conveyor System
text:
Optional signal investigations
The internally routed model does not require an external colour signal. The following investigations are relevant only if you want to inspect the component in more detail or if a later PLC extension is assigned.
To expose the Pusher Conveyor’s built-in product detector as a Boolean signal:

Add a BooleanSignal behavior named PartDetected.
Open the ComponentPathSensor behavior.
Set its BoolSignal property to PartDetected.
Run products through the pusher and verify the signal transition.

You can also investigate the Conveyor Sensor component’s RGB detection:

Add the sensor to an ordinary conveyor and reset the simulation.
Open the sensor’s RGB properties and enable colour detection.
Place one of the coloured template cylinders inside the detection area.
Select Teach in color 1.
Repeat for the remaining colours and observe the resulting outputs.

The RGB sensor reads the simulated material in its detection area, not the product-type name. Therefore, verify its outputs with products generated by the feeder before using them in control logic. RGB detection does not replace the product-type routing used in the required model.

title: Frames and Poses
text:
Many robot tasks are about motion and positioning. A tool has to approach a part, a gripper has to align with a handle, a camera has to measure a workpiece, or a pallet has to be placed relative to a fixture. To program and debug these tasks, we need tools for describing positions and orientations in space.
Consider the cell in the figure below. A camera observes a tray of small objects, and the robot has to move its gripper to a pick pose for one selected cube. To make that work, the robot program needs answers to questions such as: Where is the camera relative to the robot? Where is the selected cube relative to the camera? Where should the gripper be relative to the cube?
The concrete problem is that the robot does not directly know where the part is: the camera detects the part, but the camera and the robot do not use the same coordinate system. The robot expects TCP motion targets in its base frame, so the part pose reported in the camera frame must be converted into the robot base frame.

  
    
    
      
        
          
        
        
          
        
        
          
        
      
      
        
        
        
        
        base frame
      
      
        
        
        
        
        TCP frame
      
      
        
        
        
        
        camera frame
      
      
        
        
        
        
        part frame
      
    
  
  A camera-guided pick cell. The overlaid coordinate frames show the reference systems attached to the robot base, camera, selected part, and gripper TCP.

This example already contains the two basic ideas of the page:

A coordinate frame is a local reference system with an origin and axis directions. In the figure, frames are attached to the robot base, camera, selected part, and gripper.
A pose describes the position and orientation of one frame relative to another frame. For example, the camera has a pose relative to the robot base.

For robot tools, the important tool point is usually called the TCP: the tool center point. In the equations below, part is used as a short name for the selected workpiece frame.
A point is only a position. It can describe where a hole, corner, or detected feature is. A pose is stronger: it describes both position and orientation. A welding torch, gripper, camera, screwdriver, or dispensing nozzle must be at the right place and point in the right direction. Position is the “where”. Orientation is the “which way”.
Different robot systems expose poses in different formats. At this point, treat these formats as compact ways of writing a 3D position plus a 3D orientation. Section 3 explains the idea of a pose, and Section 3.3 returns to the practical difference between matrix notation, KUKA target values, and Universal Robots pose values.
In this page we use the notation from Corke (Corke 2023): T denotes a pose represented as a homogeneous transformation matrix. We will not derive all the matrix equations. The goal is to understand what the matrices mean and how they are used in practical robot programs.

title: Frames and Poses
section: Inverting the direction of a pose
text:
Inverting the direction of a pose
Sometimes the pose is known in the opposite direction from the one we need. If we know \({}^{base}\!T_{camera}\), we can compute \({}^{camera}\!T_{base}\) by inverting the transform:
\[
{}^{camera}T_{base} =
\left({}^{base}T_{camera}\right)^{-1}
\]
This is not just “put a minus sign on the position”. The orientation must also be inverted, and the translation must be interpreted in the rotated frame. The matrix form in Section 3.3 shows why. In practice, use the robot controller, simulation tool, or robotics library to invert poses. The important point is to recognize when the pose direction you have is not the pose direction you need.
Typical uses include converting a camera detection into the robot base frame, converting between fixture or workobject frames and the base frame, and checking where the robot base would appear from a camera or tool frame.

title: Frames and Poses
text:
A short 2D version
Real industrial robots move in 3D. Still, a 2D top-view example is a useful training step because it keeps the same logic with fewer numbers.
In 2D, a pose has three coordinates:
\[
x, \quad y, \quad \theta
\]
where x and y describe the position and theta describes the rotation of the frame. The corresponding homogeneous transformation matrix is:
\[
{}^{A}T_B =
\begin{bmatrix}
{\color{#c2410c}\cos \theta} & {\color{#c2410c}-\sin \theta} & {\color{#1d4f8e}x} \\
{\color{#c2410c}\sin \theta} & {\color{#c2410c}\cos \theta} & {\color{#2a9d8f}y} \\
0           &  0           & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
The first two columns describe orientation. The last column describes position. The last row is a mathematical trick used by homogeneous coordinates: it is always zeros followed by a 1, and it lets rotations and translations be combined in one matrix multiplication. For this course, you can use that last row as a fixed pattern without worrying too much about its derivation.
The demo below lets you explore the same matrix directly. Frame A stays fixed, while frame B is moved by changing x, y, and theta. The matrix shows how those three pose coordinates enter the transform. Use the direction buttons to switch between \({}^{A}T_B\) and the inverse pose \({}^{B}T_A\).

JavaScript is required to use the 2D transform demo.

title: Frames and Poses
text:
The 3D version used in robotics
In 3D, the same idea becomes a 4 by 4 homogeneous transformation matrix. A pose of frame B expressed in frame A is commonly written as:
\[
{}^{A}T_B =
\begin{bmatrix}
{\color{#0f766e}r_{11}} & {\color{#0f766e}r_{12}} & {\color{#0f766e}r_{13}} & {\color{#7c2d12}x} \\
{\color{#0f766e}r_{21}} & {\color{#0f766e}r_{22}} & {\color{#0f766e}r_{23}} & {\color{#7c2d12}y} \\
{\color{#0f766e}r_{31}} & {\color{#0f766e}r_{32}} & {\color{#0f766e}r_{33}} & {\color{#7c2d12}z} \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
{\color{#0f766e}R} & {\color{#7c2d12}t} \\
0\;0\;0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Here:

the brown vector t = [x, y, z]^T is the position of the origin of frame B, measured in frame A,
the teal block R is a 3 by 3 rotation matrix that describes the orientation of frame B, measured in frame A,
the bottom row is the same homogeneous-coordinate trick: zeros followed by a 1.

A useful way to read the rotation matrix is column by column:
\[
R =
\begin{bmatrix}
| & | & | \\
{}^{A}\hat{x}_{B} & {}^{A}\hat{y}_{B} & {}^{A}\hat{z}_{B} \\
| & | & |
\end{bmatrix}
\]
The first column tells where the x axis of frame B points, expressed using frame A coordinates. The second and third columns do the same for the y and z axes. These three axis directions must be perpendicular and have unit length; otherwise the matrix no longer represents a valid rigid-body orientation.
Rotation is the part where formats differ most. Position is straightforward: three distances along three axes. Orientation is harder because a 3D rotation is not just three independent distances. The order of rotations matters, different parameter sets can describe the same physical orientation, and some representations become awkward near certain orientations. This is why robot controllers, simulation tools, and vision systems do not all display orientation in the same way.
Common representations include:

Rotation matrix: good for calculation and frame chaining, but it uses nine numbers for only three rotational degrees of freedom. The columns also have to remain perpendicular unit vectors, so it is not a convenient format to type by hand.
Euler, roll-pitch-yaw, or ABC angles: compact and often easier to read on a teach pendant, but the result depends on the chosen rotation order. These formats can also have singular cases and angle wraparound, for example near +180 and -180 degrees.
Rotation vector / axis-angle: compact and useful in robot software. The vector direction gives the rotation axis and the vector length gives the rotation angle, usually in radians. The three numbers are not separate rotations about x, y, and z, so they are less intuitive to edit by hand.
Unit quaternion: common in simulation, 3D graphics, and interpolation, but it uses four numbers with a unit-length constraint, and q and -q describe the same orientation.

This is also why KUKA and Universal Robots do not just use different names for the same thing. KUKA targets commonly use X, Y, Z, A, B, C, where A, B, and C are angle-sequence orientation values. Universal Robots uses p[x, y, z, rx, ry, rz], where rx, ry, and rz form a rotation vector. In this page we write poses as transformation matrices because matrices make frame chaining and inversion easy to see. In a real robot program, the same pose may be shown as ABC angles, a rotation vector, or another orientation format, and the controller or software library converts between these representations.
With the matrix blocks above, the inverse pose from the previous section is:
\[
{}^{B}T_A = \left({}^{A}T_B\right)^{-1}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
R^T & -R^T t \\
0\;0\;0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
This is the matrix reason why inverting a pose is not just changing the sign of the translation. The translation also has to be expressed in the inverted orientation.
The demo below shows the same pose idea in 3D. Frame A stays fixed, while frame B is moved with position sliders and roll-pitch-yaw sliders. Use the direction buttons to switch between \({}^{A}T_B\) and the inverse pose \({}^{B}T_A\). The sliders are only one convenient display format for orientation; the matrix below the plot is the pose representation used for chaining and inversion.

JavaScript is required to use the 3D transform demo.

title: Robot cell
text:
In this part of the project, you will build and program a simulated robot cell in Visual Components (VC) and then coordinate it with a PLC program running in CODESYS Control Win SL. The cell transports a raw part to a robot, loads it into a CNC mill, waits for machining, unloads it, and returns the finished part to a conveyor.
This page guides you through the work in the intended order, from assembling and testing the VC-only cell to connecting and commissioning the PLC-controlled version. Use it as a working tutorial: later steps build on the checks completed in the earlier steps.
The work is divided into two stages:

Build and program a complete working cell using internal VC signals.
Transfer overall cell coordination to a PLC connected through OPC UA.

Do not begin with the PLC connection. First establish that the robot poses, motions, gripper, CNC model, and complete material flow work inside VC. This gives you a known-working plant before communication and distributed control are introduced.
By completing the project, you should be able to:

configure a robot, gripper, conveyor, sensor, and process machine in VC,
divide a robot task into meaningful reusable subroutines,
define a clear control boundary between a PLC and robot controller,
design two controllers that coordinate through a command handshake,
connect CODESYS and VC using OPC UA, and
commission the system incrementally rather than debugging everything at once.

title: Robot cell
text:
Organize the project with sublayouts
Build the robot cell in the same VC file as the completed conveyor system, but do not connect the two systems yet. Begin from the conveyor checkpoint and keep its saved copy unchanged as a tested backup. Place the new robot cell some distance away from the conveyor system, with enough empty space that the two material flows remain clearly separate during development.
The conveyor-system instructions create a Conveyor system sublayout. Confirm that the completed conveyor components are assigned to it, then create a second sublayout named Robot cell. Components for the new cell are moved into this second sublayout after their initial placement.
The roles of the Cell Graph, components, and sublayouts are introduced in Layouts and components. This structure keeps the complete system in one simulation while making each section easier to select, move, copy, and inspect. The linked section also contains the relevant VC Academy lesson. Sublayout visibility is an organizational aid; hiding a sublayout does not replace disconnecting or stopping components when you want to test only one part of the system.

title: Robot cell
text:
Design the robot cell
Start with the Simple Robot Pedestal and the KUKA robot. Place the pedestal in the 3D world and position the robot on top; you can use the attach tool to be able to move them together. The height of the pedestal can be adjusted as needed, and it is part of the cell design: it determines whether the robot can approach the conveyor and CNC at useful joint configurations, not only whether the TCP can reach them at all.
Next, add a short incoming conveyor and place a Conveyor Sensor close to its downstream end. This sensor defines the repeatable pickup location. Copy and paste the Advanced Feeder that is already configured in the conveyor system, and configure only this copy to generate grey cylinders. Keep the original mixed feeder unchanged in the Conveyor system sublayout. The temporary feeder provides test parts immediately while the robot cell is developed on its own.
Place the CNC mill and outgoing conveyor provisionally. Their first positions do not need to be final. Leave enough room to open and access the CNC door, and provide clearance for the gripper, workpiece, and approach and retract motions.
The final cell layout is your design decision, and there is no prescribed arrangement. Among the choices are the relative positions and orientations of the robot, conveyors, CNC mill, and access areas. For example, the conveyors could be arranged in line or at an angle, and the CNC mill could be placed beside the robot or across from the conveyors. These are only starting points; you may develop another arrangement that gives a good combination of robot reach, clear motion paths, material flow, and access to the equipment.

Check reachability and clearance
The VC reachability overview explains how workspace profiles, jogging, joint checks, and collision detection complement one another.
Use the robot’s WorkSpace2D or WorkSpace3D component properties to display its approximate workspace, also called its work envelope. Use this envelope as rough guidance for the initial cell layout and for estimating basic distances between the robot, conveyors, and CNC mill. Figure 1 shows the WorkSpace2D profile around the Agilus robot used in this project. The linked VC overview contains the relevant Academy lessons.
This profile approximates position reach; it does not prove that the robot can achieve the required tool orientation at every point. The distinction between reachable and dexterous workspace explains why checking the complete task poses is necessary.






Figure 1: The approximate WorkSpace2D profile of the KUKA KR6 R900 Agilus displayed in Visual Components.



For more detailed and reliable tuning of the arrangement, mount the gripper (see Section 4.3 for how to mount and use it), generate one grey cylinder, and grip it. Then use the Jog tool to move the complete robot, tool, and workpiece assembly through the important task poses. After all, it is the workpiece that must be placed at the positions and orientations required by the task. The cell must therefore allow the robot to move the workpiece through these poses without exceeding joint limits, approaching singularities, or colliding with the surrounding equipment. While jogging, use the Jog panel to monitor each joint’s current value and permitted range. This shows when a target pose pushes one or more joints toward their limits. Enable Color Highlight in the Limits group to also mark the affected robot geometry in red when a joint limit is exceeded. Enable a collision detector and start the simulation once to initialize it. You can then reset the simulation and use the detector while jogging; collisions with the CNC, conveyors, pedestal, and other equipment are highlighted in yellow in the 3D view.
Manual jogging checks individual poses but does not validate every point along the programmed motion between them. After teaching representative motions, run the program with collision detection and the Limits tools enabled, including the singularity check.
Before teaching the complete program, verify that:

the robot can reach the pickup, CNC loading, outgoing conveyor, and home poses,
the gripper and workpiece fit through the CNC opening,
the robot can approach and retract without crossing the machine or fence,
the conveyor sensor is located at a repeatable pickup pose.

These checks are easier to correct before many robot positions depend on the layout.


Consider safety while the layout develops
Do not wait until the end of the project to think about safety, but also do not spend time drawing final fencing while the equipment is still moving between tests. During layout design, consider where people need access for loading, teaching, clearing faults, and maintenance; where parts and people could enter the cell intentionally or unintentionally; where a gate could be placed; and whether robot motion creates trapping points against the CNC mill, fence, or other fixed equipment.
Once the equipment positions are mostly stable and the relevant robot motions have been checked, use the Fence and Wall Builder from Facilities - Factory to draw the perimeter caging. This is usually the most convenient way to create and revise the fence. Simulation does not replace a risk assessment, but it makes alternative layouts easier to examine before positions and control logic become difficult to change. The safety process and the priority given to reducing hazards through design are discussed in the risk-assessment process and the risk-reduction priorities on the robot safety page.
After placing the cell equipment, select the newly added components and use Move to Layout to assign them to the Robot cell sublayout. Check the Layouts tab afterwards to make sure that no cell component remains at the ROOT level. Moving the components together is usually quicker than assigning each component immediately after adding it.

title: Robot cell
text:
Mount and configure the gripper
Mount the Generic 3 Finger Gripper directly on the robot flange using PnP. Move the gripper toward the flange until the compatible physical interfaces are highlighted, then continue moving it until the components snap together. This physical connection makes the gripper follow the flange when the robot is jogged. The Add a robot tool chapter in the Introduction to Robot Teaching video demonstrates this workflow.
Enable automatic I/O connection when mounting the gripper. This option is enabled by default and avoids having to connect the gripper’s input and output signals to the robot manually.
Before configuring these signals, it is important to understand how standard grasping works in VC. A grasp action searches for products inside a detection volume around a selected tool frame. When a product is found, VC fixes its pose relative to that frame, so the product moves with the robot. A release action removes this logical attachment. Physical finger contact is not calculated, which is why VC can grasp a product even when no gripper model is mounted or the fingers do not touch it. VC also provides rigid-body physics for custom contact-based simulations, but that is a separate, more complex approach and is not used in this project.
The finger animation is therefore not what holds the product in the standard simulation, but it is still important. Realistic open and closed widths let you check the gripper’s geometric capacity and its clearance around the workpiece. They also make collision checking more meaningful because an open gripper occupies a different volume from a closed one. Visible finger motion helps you understand and debug the program sequence, and it makes the simulation clearer and more convincing in customer or sales presentations. It does not validate real gripping force, payload capacity, deformation, or slip.
The general relationship between robot I/O ports, component signals, and Actions Configuration is introduced in Robot I/O and signal actions. The configuration below applies those mechanisms specifically to the project gripper.
The logical grasp and release actions are configured in the robot’s Actions Configuration properties. In most VC robot components, outputs 1 to 16 are predefined for grasping and releasing with the default tool frames. These outputs can be used for a tool without movable joints, such as a suction cup, or even without a visible gripper. In that case, the output does not need to be connected to another component: setting it only triggers the robot’s internal grasp or release action. Always inspect the selected robot’s mappings because component models can differ.
A gripper with movable fingers requires both parts of the simulation. The robot output must trigger VC’s internal grasp or release action and drive the gripper joint so that the fingers close or open. After mounting the gripper, inspect its Control properties and the robot’s signal connections. Automatically connected custom gripper I/O commonly starts at robot port 100.
In the tested cell, robot output 100 is connected to the gripper input IN_J1_Action: TRUE closes the fingers and FALSE opens them. Configure the same output in Actions Configuration so that TRUE also performs Grasp and FALSE performs Release. Select a tool frame at the centre of the gripping region and set a detection volume that contains the cylinder at the grasp pose without including nearby products. It is usually easiest to align one of the robot’s native tool frames with the gripper’s TCP after mounting the gripper, and then use that frame for both the grasp action and the robot motion statements. Figure 2 shows the signal connection and action configuration together. Section 4.4 explains the TCP setup in more detail.






Figure 2: Robot output 100 is connected to the movable gripper and configured to perform the internal VC grasp and release actions using Tool_TCP.



Opening and closing the gripper takes time. After commanding it, read its separate open-state or closed-state feedback and wait until the requested state has been reached before moving the robot. The Test the signals chapter in the Model a robot gripper, part II lesson demonstrates this I/O and feedback workflow.
Finally, use VC’s measure tool to determine the cylinder size and set the gripper’s J1_OpenValue and J1_CloseValue properties accordingly. Run the sequence and confirm that the fingers fully clear the cylinder when open and close to a realistic gripping width.

title: Robot cell
text:
Define and select the TCP
The attached gripper contributes a TCP frame. Select a frame located at the centre of the gripping region and use it as the active tool frame in the robot motion statements. Inspect its position and orientation rather than assuming that the component’s default frame is suitable. If necessary, move one of the robot’s native tool frames to the required TCP and use that frame consistently throughout the program.
The frame should be located and oriented according to the physical task, not only at a convenient point in the 3D model. Review frames and poses if the TCP or reference-frame behavior is unclear.

text:
CNC mill
Use the Process Machine - CNC component. Configure a short process time during development and inspect its command and feedback signals:

There is no separate process-complete signal in this model. The controller must first observe ProcessIsRunning = TRUE and then wait for it to return to FALSE. Waiting only for FALSE could incorrectly report completion before the process has started.

title: Robot cell
text:
Use meaningful subroutines
Do not write the complete task as one long Main routine. At minimum, organize the motions into operations corresponding to:

picking a part from the conveyor,
moving to and loading the CNC,
running the CNC process,
unloading the CNC and placing the finished part, and
returning home.

Choose names that describe what each operation achieves. Each routine should start and finish in a predictable situation and contain the details tightly coupled to that operation. For example, the pick routine should operate the gripper and verify its feedback before retracting.
The internal Main routine should read like the material flow rather than a list of individual robot motions. This makes the program easier to test now and provides subroutines that can be requested by the PLC later.

title: Robot cell
text:
Validate before continuing
Run repeated complete cycles and verify:

all robot positions and configurations are reachable,
approach and retract paths do not collide,
the correct base and tool frames are active,
the gripper reaches its commanded state before the next motion,
the part is attached and released at the expected points,
the CNC door and process sequence completes correctly, and
the robot ends each cycle at a known home pose.

Do not proceed to external PLC control until this version works reliably.

title: Robot cell
text:
Moving equipment after teaching positions
If you must relocate or rotate the robot after teaching positions, change Lock Positions from To reference to To World before moving it. Change the setting back afterwards. This holds the taught poses fixed in the world while the robot base moves.
For equipment-relative tasks, consider defining robot base frames on the relevant equipment instead. A pose defined relative to a CNC fixture then moves with that fixture, which can make later layout changes easier. Choose the method that reflects which physical relationship should remain fixed.

title: Robot cell
section: Integrate the conveyor and robot-cell sublayouts
text:
Integrate the conveyor and robot-cell sublayouts
After the internally controlled robot program works reliably with the temporary feeder, connect the two subsystems. Disconnect or remove the robot cell’s feeder, move the Conveyor system and Robot cell sublayouts together, and connect the appropriate conveyor paths. Start the original mixed feeder in the Conveyor system sublayout only after this connection is working.
Run the complete material flow again before adding PLC control. Check not only whether the robot cycle still runs, but also whether parts queue at the expected locations, whether upstream conveyors become blocked, and whether the timing between part arrival, conveyor stopping, and robot pickup remains reliable.

title: Robot cell
text:
Two interacting state machines
A finite-state machine (FSM) organizes a sequence into a small number of states. At any moment, one state is active. That state describes what the controller is doing or waiting for, and a defined event causes the transition to another state. Here, states such as Ready, Busy, and Done describe the status of the command interface. They are not robot poses.
Use a state machine on each side of the interface, but at different levels:

The PLC FSM represents progress through the complete material flow and decides which device may act next.
The robot-side FSM accepts one operation request, executes the selected robot subroutine, and reports its status.







flowchart LR
    PLC[PLC cell FSM]
    CONVEYOR[Ordinary conveyors and pickup sensor]
    CNC[CNC mill]

    subgraph VC[VC robot program]
        ROBOT[Command-interface FSM]
        ROUTINES[Motion and gripper subroutines]
        ROBOT -->|Call operation| ROUTINES
    end

    PLC -->|Command| ROBOT
    ROBOT -->|State and active command| PLC
    PLC -->|Run| CONVEYOR
    CONVEYOR -->|Part detected| PLC
    PLC -->|Door and process commands| CNC
    CNC -->|Door and process feedback| PLC




Figure 3: The PLC coordinates the cell, while the robot-side state machine turns each accepted command into one complete robot operation.





The arrows in Figure 3 show the division of responsibility and the information exchanged between the controllers. The command sequence inside the robot-side FSM is shown in Figure 4. In the normal path, the robot repeatedly accepts one command, executes it, and waits until the PLC acknowledges completion before becoming ready again.
The figure focuses on the PLC-to-robot interface. The Pusher Conveyor’s local routing and transfer behavior remains inside VC as described earlier and is not part of this command exchange.






stateDiagram-v2
    direction LR
    state "Invalid command" as InvalidCommand
    [*] --> Initializing
    Initializing --> Ready: Initialization complete<br/>and Command = 0
    Ready --> Busy: Valid command accepted
    Busy --> Done: Robot subroutine complete
    Done --> Ready: Command = 0<br/>acknowledgement
    Ready --> InvalidCommand: Non-zero Command<br/>outside 1 to 4
    InvalidCommand --> Ready: Command = 0




Figure 4: States and transitions of the robot command interface, including rejection of an undefined command.





The PLC must not calculate robot joint motion, and the robot must not silently continue the complete production sequence after one requested operation. Both controllers should be understandable and testable independently.

title: Robot cell
text:
Robot command properties
To realize the robot-side FSM in the VC Program Editor, the robot program needs values through which it can receive a request and report its current state. A local program line or routine name is not automatically visible to CODESYS. Component properties solve this problem: the robot program can read and write them in expressions, and VC Connectivity can map them to PLC variables through OPC UA. Together, the properties form a small command-and-status interface between the two state machines.
On the VC Modeling tab, add three integer properties to the robot component and place them in a group named PLC. Set the initial value of all three properties to 0:








Property
Direction
Purpose




PLC::Command
PLC to robot
The robot’s request input. The PLC writes the number of the operation it wants; zero means no active request.


PLC::RobotState
Robot to PLC
The robot’s status output. The robot program writes the current interface state so the PLC knows whether it may send, wait, or continue.


PLC::ActiveCommand
Robot to PLC
The robot’s latched-command output. The robot copies a non-zero request here and keeps it while that request is being checked and handled.



PLC is only the property-group name. In a robot-program expression, the :: syntax separates the group and property names.
The ownership of the properties is deliberate: the PLC writes Command, while the robot writes RobotState and ActiveCommand. Command is the request that has arrived from outside the robot program. ActiveCommand is the robot’s latched record and echo of that request. For a valid request, it identifies the operation throughout both Busy and Done, lets the PLC verify what was accepted and completed, and prevents an unexpected later change to Command from changing the operation already underway. For an undefined request, ActiveCommand identifies the rejected value while RobotState = 4 reports that it was not accepted. The robot should therefore select an operation from ActiveCommand, not continuously from the externally written Command.
Use the following interface contract:



Command
Required robot operation




0
No active request


1
Pick the part from the conveyor


2
Load the CNC


3
Unload the CNC and place the part on the conveyor


4
Move to the home pose






Robot state
Meaning




0
Initializing


1
Ready for a command


2
Busy executing the accepted command


3
Command completed and waiting for acknowledgement


4
Invalid command




Example: requesting the load operation
Suppose the robot reports RobotState = 1, meaning Ready, and the PLC wants it to load the CNC:

The PLC writes Command = 2 and keeps that value active.
The robot detects the request, checks that 2 is valid, copies it to ActiveCommand, and changes RobotState to 2 (Busy).
The PLC waits until it sees ActiveCommand = 2 together with a robot state of Busy or Done. ActiveCommand identifies which request was accepted, while the state confirms that the robot accepted it. Together, these values form the robot acceptance confirmation.
The robot selects the case for ActiveCommand = 2 and calls the subroutine that loads the CNC.
When the subroutine returns, the robot changes RobotState to 3 (Done) while ActiveCommand remains 2.
After seeing Done for the expected active command, the PLC writes Command = 0. This is the PLC completion acknowledgement.
The robot clears ActiveCommand and returns RobotState to 1 (Ready).

This exchange lets the PLC coordinate the overall process without controlling the individual robot motions. It also prevents the robot from starting the next production step on its own.

title: Robot cell
section: Implement the robot-side FSM in VC
text:
Implement the robot-side FSM in VC
VC does not provide a special state-machine object. Build the FSM in the robot program from property assignments, conditions, loops, routine calls, and either If/Else or Switch Case statements. The VC program-structure section introduces these statements and links to the relevant VC lessons and documentation.
The state diagram defines the observable behavior of the interface; it does not require one Switch Case with one case for every state. A simpler implementation uses the order of statements in a repeating loop to move through the states. RobotState then reports where that sequence currently is, while one Switch Case on ActiveCommand selects the requested robot operation.
In the VC Program Editor, use Set Property statements for assignments such as PLC::ActiveCommand = PLC::Command and PLC::RobotState = 2. The following outline follows this sequential implementation. It adds an explicit validity check before reporting Busy, so an undefined command cannot briefly appear to have been accepted. The outline illustrates the structure; it is not source code that can be pasted into VC.
Set Property: PLC::RobotState = 0 (Initializing)
Set Property: PLC::ActiveCommand = 0
perform the required initialization

While PLC::Command is not 0
  Delay 0.05 s
Set Property: PLC::RobotState = 1 (Ready)

While the robot program is running
  While PLC::Command is 0
    Delay 0.05 s

  Set Property: PLC::ActiveCommand = PLC::Command

  If PLC::ActiveCommand is in the range 1 to 4
    Set Property: PLC::RobotState = 2 (Busy)

    Switch Case PLC::ActiveCommand
      Case 1: call the pick subroutine
      Case 2: call the load subroutine
      Case 3: call the unload subroutine
      Case 4: call the home subroutine

    Set Property: PLC::RobotState = 3 (Done)
  Else
    Set Property: PLC::RobotState = 4 (Invalid command)

  While PLC::Command is not 0
    Delay 0.05 s

  Set Property: PLC::ActiveCommand = 0
  Set Property: PLC::RobotState = 1 (Ready)
The first waiting loop holds Ready until a command arrives. The robot then latches and checks the request. For values 1 to 4, it reports Busy and selects one operation from ActiveCommand. Because a call does not return until its subroutine has finished, the next assignment changes the state to Done. An undefined value instead changes the state directly from Ready to Invalid command without calling a motion routine. In both paths, the last waiting loop holds the result until the PLC clears Command.
Each robot operation remains a separate subroutine, so the dispatcher is easy to read and the motions can still be tested independently. An explicit state-driven Switch Case is also possible, but it adds another level of nesting without improving this small interface.
State 4 only handles an undefined command in the required implementation. It does not automatically detect a failed robot motion or an unsuccessful grip. Detecting such failures, reporting them, and defining a safe recovery sequence belong to the optional timeout and fault-handling extension.

title: Robot cell
text:
Required command handshake
The load example above can be generalized into the following reusable protocol. For every robot operation:

The PLC waits for robot state Ready.
The PLC writes and holds the requested command.
The robot copies it to ActiveCommand and reports Busy as its acceptance confirmation.
The PLC verifies the matching ActiveCommand. It accepts either Busy or Done as proof that the command was accepted.
The robot executes the complete subroutine and reports Done.
After observing Done with the matching ActiveCommand, the PLC clears Command to 0 as its completion acknowledgement.
The robot clears ActiveCommand and returns to Ready.

Busy is useful for monitoring, but the PLC must not depend on observing it. A short robot routine could reach Done between two OPC UA updates. The held ActiveCommand and Done values still prove which operation completed.
This level-based handshake is preferable to short pulses because a pulse could be missed between an OPC UA update and a PLC scan.






Tip



VC robot programs provide a dedicated wait statement only for binary robot inputs. To wait for an integer component property, use a While loop with a short delay, for example 0.05 s. The loop condition should describe when the program must continue waiting. The delay prevents an empty polling loop from consuming simulation execution time. Use such delayed waits in the Ready, Done, and invalid-command parts of the sequential loop shown above.

title: Robot Safety
text:
Industrial robots can remove people from heavy, repetitive, dirty, and dangerous work. At the same time, a robot cell combines powerful motion, automatic control, tools, workpieces, and other machinery. Safe automation therefore depends on the complete application and on how people actually work with it, not only on the robot arm.
Robot safety is not a feature that can be added after the cell has been designed. It is a chain of decisions connecting the work people need to perform with the layout, equipment, control system, working procedures, and checks on the finished installation. A useful question throughout this process is:
The first half of the question directs attention to people, tasks, access, and unusual situations such as cleaning or fault recovery. The second half requires a concrete explanation of how the danger is removed, separated, detected, limited, or otherwise controlled. That explanation must still make sense when equipment fails, someone needs access, or the application changes.
A hazard is something with the potential to cause harm. Risk describes how serious that harm could be and how likely it is to occur in the situation being considered. A robot can remain a hazard even when protective measures have reduced the associated risk.
A risk assessment is the structured and documented process used to work through this reasoning. You examine the tasks and people involved, identify hazards and possible harm, decide where further risk reduction is needed, and record the assumptions behind those decisions. Risk reduction then changes the design or adds protective measures. The finished measures must be implemented, tested, maintained, and reconsidered when the cell or its use changes. This is the overall safety process that the rest of the page develops.

title: Robot Safety
text:
Normal I/O and safety I/O
Ordinary I/O is used for production information and commands: a part-present sensor, a cycle-start request, a completed-operation signal, or a lamp on the operator panel. Safety I/O carries signals that form part of a safety function, such as an interlocked-gate state, a scanner protective field, a safeguard-stop request, or confirmation that a monitored safe state is active.







Normal control
Safety-related control




Usually processed by the standard PLC program or robot task program
Processed by a safety relay, safety PLC, or built-in robot safety controller


Intended to control and coordinate production
Intended to achieve a specified protective response


A wiring, communication, or program fault can produce an incorrect value without the diagnostics needed for a safety role
Uses suitable monitoring and diagnostics so relevant faults cause or maintain the specified safe response


Useful for status, orderly stopping, sequencing, and messages
Used for the safety function itself when the assessment requires a dependable response



Safety I/O commonly uses monitored channel pairs. The exact architecture depends on the equipment and required function. A normal input does not become safety-related because it is read twice, and an ordinary robot-program if statement does not become safety logic because the variable is named safe.
Safety-related data can be carried over the same industrial network as ordinary control data by using a dedicated safety communication protocol. Examples include PROFIsafe with PROFINET or PROFIBUS, CIP Safety with EtherNet/IP, and FSoE, short for Fail Safe over EtherCAT, with EtherCAT. These protocols do not assume that the underlying network is free from faults. Instead, the safety layer at the sending and receiving devices checks information such as message identity, order, timing, and integrity. Sharing the physical network does not make ordinary fieldbus data safety-related.

title: Robot Safety
section: Where is the safety logic implemented?
text:
Where is the safety logic implemented?
Robot cells often distribute safety-related control across several devices:

The robot safety controller supervises built-in robot functions such as stops, monitored standstill (a stopped state supervised by the safety controller), speed or position limits, and configured safety inputs and outputs.
A safety relay can implement a small number of fixed functions, such as connecting one interlocked gate to stop inputs.
A safety PLC is useful when several guards, scanners, operating modes, robots, conveyors, positioners, or process machines must be coordinated.
The standard PLC still manages the production sequence, displays status, requests orderly actions, and starts the process only after the safety system permits operation and the normal process conditions are satisfied.

Some PLC platforms can execute the standard control program and a separately managed safety program in the same controller or industrial PC. Such a system can connect to both standard I/O modules and safety-rated I/O modules, sometimes mounted side by side in the same modular I/O station. Production sensors and actuators normally use the standard modules, while devices and outputs that form part of a safety function use suitable safety modules. Sharing a controller, engineering environment, backplane, or network does not remove this distinction. Where a response is required for safety, it must not depend only on ordinary PLC code, ordinary fieldbus data, or the robot’s task program.
Figure 1 shows one possible hardware arrangement. In this example, the safety logic is implemented in a dedicated TwinSAFE logic terminal; other Beckhoff architectures can execute the safety program in a safety runtime on an industrial PC.






Figure 1: A Beckhoff EtherCAT terminal station with grey standard I/O terminals and yellow TwinSAFE safety input, output, and logic terminals. The modules can be mounted together, but standard and safety-related signal processing remain distinct. Image excerpt from the Beckhoff EL2904 operating instructions.



A robot stop also does not automatically stop the rest of the cell. A gripper may retain stored pneumatic energy, a positioner may continue moving, or a process machine may remain hazardous. The safety function therefore needs a clear span of control: the robot and every other item of equipment that must respond to that input.

title: Robot Safety
section: Example: requesting access through an interlocked gate
text:
Example: requesting access through an interlocked gate
A simple cell can use the following sequence:

The operator requests access. The standard PLC can finish the current step and request an orderly process stop.
The gate switch is monitored through safety I/O. Opening the gate activates the safety logic even if the ordinary sequence has not stopped correctly.
The safety logic commands the robot and every other relevant hazard into the specified safe state.
Hazardous operation remains inhibited while the gate is open.
Closing the gate restores the safeguard but does not restart the cell. A deliberate reset confirms that the protective arrangement is restored.
A separate start command is required before automatic production resumes.

If a person can enter fully and remain hidden inside the cell, closing the gate and pressing reset may not be sufficient. The design can require visibility from the reset position, presence detection, a trapped-key arrangement, or another measure selected for the actual access situation.
As one vendor example, current UR controllers provide dedicated and configurable safety I/O for functions such as safeguard stop, emergency stop, reduced mode, and safety status. The UR Safety I/O documentation also shows an interlocked-door example. Other robot and PLC platforms use different terminals, software, and communication systems, but the same input-logic-output reasoning applies.

title: Robot Safety
Robot Safety
text:
Changes after handover
Handover is not the end of the process. A new tool, payload, fixture, product, program, operating mode, access point, or surrounding machine can invalidate an earlier assumption. Review such changes before production resumes. Substantial rebuilding can also affect who carries the responsibilities of a machine manufacturer; see Arbeidstilsynet’s guidance for machinery production and modification.

title: Simulation
text:
Before a robot cell exists, many decisions already have to be made. Can the robot reach all required poses? Is there enough space for the tool and workpiece? Will the cell meet the required cycle time? How should the robot, conveyors, sensors, and PLC coordinate? Building the cell first and answering these questions afterwards is slow, expensive, and difficult to change.
A simulation lets you investigate such questions using an executable model of the planned or existing system. You can change the model, run an experiment, observe the result, and compare alternatives without immediately changing the real equipment. This makes simulation useful for robot motion, complete cells, production lines, training, and communication with customers and operators. Here, executable means that the model changes over time: components move, signals change, and the modeled equipment responds according to defined behavior. A static 3D drawing can be part of a simulation model, but it is not a simulation by itself.
Consider a palletizing cell in which a robot picks boxes from a conveyor and places them on pallets. A simulation could help select the robot and gripper, develop the layout, check reachability and collisions, estimate cycle time and production capacity, and test how the PLC sequence responds to missing boxes, full pallets, or stopped equipment. The same model can also make the proposed cell easier to discuss with the customer and the people who will operate it.
These are not all the same simulation problem. A rough layout may be sufficient for checking floor space, while cycle-time prediction or testing connected control software needs much more detailed behavior. The purpose of the simulation therefore determines what must be included in the model.
The questions above are not only technical checks. Together, they can provide an early proof of concept before investing in the robot, tooling, fixtures, sensors, safety equipment, engineering, and installation. The simulation helps show whether a concept deserves further development and which uncertain parts still need more investigation.
These technical results can support the business case. For example, simulated cycle time and production capacity can be combined with expected production volume, labor requirements, integration costs, and operating costs to estimate payback and compare alternative concepts. Simulation does not calculate profitability by itself, but it can replace important guesses with better evidence while changes are still inexpensive.
This is where simulation connects usefully to Lean Robotics. The methodology recommends comparing the current and proposed tasks, calculating return on investment, and de-risking critical assumptions before finalizing the robotic cell concept (Bouchard 2017). Simulation is one practical tool for supporting those steps; it is not itself a Lean Robotics principle.
In this course, we use Visual Components Premium OLP 5.1 as our main environment for building robot cells, simulating production behavior, developing robot operations, and connecting simulation with PLC programming. It is one example of a simulation platform, not the only possible choice.






Important



A simulation is not automatically a correct prediction of reality. It answers a question within the assumptions and limitations of its model. A convincing 3D animation can still give a wrong result.

title: Simulation
section: Model fidelity and the simulation-to-reality gap
text:
Model fidelity and the simulation-to-reality gap
Model fidelity describes how closely the relevant behavior of the model matches the real system. Fidelity is not one overall percentage. A model can have accurate robot geometry but unrealistic sensor timing, or realistic material flow but only approximate robot motion.
Different levels of fidelity within one model are not only acceptable but often desirable. Use high fidelity where an error could change the decision, and use simpler representations where additional detail would not affect the result. This avoids spending unnecessary time, data preparation, maintenance effort, and computing resources while preserving accuracy where it matters.
The difference between simulated and real behavior is often called the simulation-to-reality gap, or simply the sim-to-real gap. In industrial robotics, common causes are inaccurate geometry, frames, payload data, or robot configurations; idealized sensors, gripping, contact, and communication; differences between generic simulated motion and the real controller; omitted process variation and recovery situations; and physical changes that were not added to the model.
The gap cannot be removed by making the graphics more realistic. It is reduced by using trustworthy input data, calibrating the real cell, comparing important simulation results with independent calculations or measurements, and updating the model when the installation changes.
Two checks are useful. Verification asks whether the model has been implemented as intended. For example, are signals connected to the correct simulated sensors, and does the gripper logic follow the specified sequence?
Validation asks whether the model represents the real system well enough for its intended use. For example, do measured robot cycle times agree closely enough with the simulated times for a production-capacity decision?
Validation is always connected to a purpose. A model validated for explaining a cell concept to a customer is not automatically accurate enough for predicting throughput or transferring a robot program.
The evidence behind a simulation should remain traceable. Record the sources and versions of important input data, the assumptions and limitations, the scenarios that were tested, and the model version used to produce the result. Relevant scenarios may include normal production, product variants, waiting conditions, and selected faults rather than only one ideal cycle.

title: Simulation
text:
Robot-level simulation
At robot level, simulation is closely connected to the concepts from frames and poses, kinematics, path planning, and motion control. Path planning determines a feasible motion between poses, while motion control governs how the robot axes follow the commanded motion. At this level, simulation is mainly used to check reachability and collisions, identify difficult joint configurations or singularities, and estimate cycle time. For process tasks, the simulated path also helps verify that the tool keeps the required orientation relative to the workpiece.
In Visual Components, this corresponds to teaching positions and building robot programs from routines and statements, with the appropriate tool and base frames. Its robot-simulation tools can then be used to inspect reachability, collisions, and cycle time. In Premium OLP, Path Check can inspect the interpolated motion between program statements; path-solving tools can also be used where the corresponding add-on is available. The Visual Components robot-simulation learning path introduces these software concepts.
For the palletizing example, the robot can reach the top of a new pallet quite easily but may struggle with the lowest boxes at the far side. A simulation lets you test the robot position, pallet orientation, tool length, and approach direction before fixing the layout.

title: Simulation
text:
Cell and production-flow simulation
At cell or production-line level, the main question is often not one robot pose but how resources interact over time. A box arrives, a sensor changes state, the PLC starts the robot, a machine finishes, or a buffer becomes full. These changes are commonly represented as events in a discrete-event simulation.
This broader model can reveal production rate, queues, buffers, bottlenecks, and resource utilization. It can also show how product variants, failures, material shortages, or coordination between processes affect the complete system.
In Visual Components, the closest counterpart is Process Modeling. A product is an item moving through production, a process defines what happens at a station, and a flow defines the sequence of processes that the product follows. The Process Flow editor is used to define this sequence, while transport links and controllers represent movement between processes. The Introduction to Process Modeling uses this vocabulary to build production-flow simulations.
A robot path that is two seconds faster may have no effect on total production if the robot is usually waiting for the upstream machine. Conversely, a small buffer may increase production more than a faster robot. Whole-cell simulation helps reveal these system-level effects.

title: Simulation
text:
Generic models and virtual controllers
A general simulation tool can calculate robot motion from a kinematic model and then translate the result through a postprocessor. This is flexible and supports many robot brands, but details such as path blending, motion timing, and special instructions may differ from the real controller.
A virtual controller runs the robot vendor’s controller software, or a closely corresponding software version, on a computer. It can provide better agreement for program syntax, configuration, motion generation, I/O behavior, and cycle time. For example, ABB describes RobotStudio as using an ABB Virtual Controller, and KUKA combines KUKA.Sim with controller and connectivity options for programming and testing a simulated cell.
Even a virtual controller does not make the complete cell real. Contact, gripping, process behavior, external equipment, communication, and mechanical variation still depend on the surrounding model.
